title: Word Break
description:
# Word Break

Given a string `s` and a dictionary `wordDict`, return `true` if `s` can be segmented into one or more dictionary words.

A segmentation must cover the whole string from left to right without skipping characters. Dictionary words may be reused any number of times. You only need to decide whether at least one valid segmentation exists; you do not need to return the words.

## Example 1

**Input:** `s = "leetcode", wordDict = ["leet","code"]`

**Output:** `true`

**Explanation:** `"leetcode"` can be segmented as `"leet code"`.

## Example 2

**Input:** `s = "applepenapple", wordDict = ["apple","pen"]`

**Output:** `true`

**Explanation:** `"apple"` can be reused, so the string can be segmented as `"apple pen apple"`.

## Example 3

**Input:** `s = "catsandog", wordDict = ["cats","dog","sand","and","cat"]`

**Output:** `false`

**Explanation:** The words overlap in useful ways, but no sequence covers every character exactly once.

## Constraints

- `1 <= s.length <= 300`
- `1 <= wordDict.length <= 1000`
- `1 <= wordDict[i].length <= 20`
- `s` and `wordDict[i]` contain only lowercase English letters
- All strings in `wordDict` are unique

solutions.name: Bottom-Up Cut DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Let `dp[end]` mean the prefix `s[0..end)` can be segmented. Store dictionary words in a hash set and track the maximum word length. For each `end`, try only possible previous cut positions within that length window.

## Key Insight

A prefix is segmentable if it can be split at some earlier reachable cut and the last block is a dictionary word. `dp[0] = true` represents the empty prefix before the first word.

## Complexity Analysis

For each end position, at most `L` previous cuts are checked, and substring creation can cost up to `L`, so the time complexity is `O(n * L^2)`, where `L` is the maximum word length. The DP table and dictionary set use `O(n + W)` space, where `W` is the number of dictionary words.

solutions.name: Forward Reachability by Words
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a boolean array `reachable`, where `reachable[start]` means a valid segmentation can end at index `start`. From every reachable cut, try every dictionary word and mark the next cut when `s` starts with that word.

## Key Insight

This is the same state graph as DP, but traversed forward from known reachable cuts. It avoids checking cuts that are not reachable and makes word reuse explicit.

## Complexity Analysis

Every reachable index may try all `W` words, and each `startsWith` check costs up to `L`, so the time complexity is `O(n * W * L)`. The reachable array uses `O(n)` space.

solutions.name: Top-Down Memoized DFS
solutions.description:
## Approach

Define `canBreak(index)` as whether the suffix beginning at `index` can be segmented. Try every possible next word ending, recurse on the remaining suffix, and memoize failed or successful indices.

## Key Insight

The recursion mirrors the natural question: choose the first word, then solve the rest. Memoization prevents repeated exploration of the same suffix after different earlier cuts.

## Complexity Analysis

There are `n` suffix states and each can try up to `n` endings. Substring lookup costs depend on substring length, so the simple bound is `O(n^2 * L)`. The memo table and dictionary set use `O(n + W)` space.

solutions.name: BFS Over Cut Positions
solutions.description:
## Approach

Treat string indices as nodes in an unweighted graph. There is an edge from `start` to `end` when `s[start..end)` is a dictionary word. BFS explores reachable cut positions and succeeds when it reaches `n`.

## Key Insight

The problem is reachability over cut positions. A visited array is essential because many different segmentations can lead to the same index.

## Complexity Analysis

There are `O(n^2)` possible substrings, and creating/checking substrings can cost up to `O(n)`, so the straightforward bound is `O(n^3)`. The queue, visited array, and dictionary set use `O(n + W)` space.

solutions.name: Trie-Accelerated Prefix DP
solutions.description:
## Approach

Insert every dictionary word into a trie. From each reachable start index, walk the trie along `s`; whenever a trie node marks a full word, mark that end index reachable.

## Key Insight

The trie lets the algorithm stop as soon as the current prefix is not shared by any dictionary word. This avoids repeatedly hashing substrings and is useful when many words share prefixes.

## Complexity Analysis

From each reachable start, the trie walk is bounded by maximum word length `L`, so the time complexity is `O(n * L)`. The reachable table uses `O(n)` space and the trie uses `O(T)` space for total dictionary characters.
